results.why: Deck B is a tighter Jeskai control shell: 4 Helix, 3 Get Lost, 4 Inevitable Defeat, 2 Day of Judgment and 6 real counters give it dense, cheap interaction, with Lute and Traumatic Critique as a sensible mana-sink top end. Deck A spends eight slots on Tablet of Discovery and Flashback, runs only 2 Helix/3 counters, and leans on 4 seven-mana Revelations, making its early game much softer against aggressive Standard decks. Both manabases are workable, but B's Verge-heavy, Great Hall-supported base covers the black splash and double-white wraths more cleanly.

Deck A is a coherent four-color instant-speed control shell: a full set of No More Lies plus Three Steps Ahead, 4 Helix, 3 Get Lost, 4 Inevitable Defeat and 2 Day of Judgment give it real density of answers, and Resonating Lute/Great Hall actually turn its many lands into Revelation and Traumatic Critique mana. Deck B is thin on interaction (3 counters, scattered 2-of burn, no Get Lost), leans on 4 Tablet of Discovery and random 1-ofs like North Wind Avatar and Flashback that don't advance a plan, and its mana base is a pile of singleton slow lands and Multiversal Passage that will stumble more often than A's shock/Verge-based 26-land base.

Deck B is an actual plan: sixteen mana dorks (including Gene Pollinator fixing for Balloon Man) ramp into Gearhulk, Ouroboroid, and Craterhoof, with Nature's Rhythm as a tutor-to-battlefield that has real targets and Balloon Man copying Craterhoof for a second overrun; it's exactly 60 and the 20-land count is fine given the dork density. Deck A is 61 cards, runs a singleton Balloon Man with essentially no red sources, plays Stormchaser's Talent with only four instants/sorceries, and has four Nature's Rhythm with no payoff worth finding—it generates mana and bounces its own Gearhulk but never converts that into a win.

Deck A is a coherent ramp-combo shell: sixteen mana creatures plus Bloom Tender/Gene Pollinator feed Nature's Rhythm and Formidable Speaker into real finishers (Craterhoof, Ouroboroid, Balloon Man copying Craterhoof/Gearhulk), and the 20-land four-color base with Starting Town, shocks, and Passages supports GGWW and the red splash well enough. Deck B is 61 cards with no closer at all—its Cam/Badgermole/Tender engine just draws cards and levels a Talent with only eight instants/sorceries, Nature's Rhythm has almost nothing worth fetching beyond Gearhulk, and the lone Jolly Balloon Man has essentially no red sources. A strong player would take the deck that actually wins games.

Deck B is the tighter, more tournament-ready build: a low curve of Dwarves, cheap efficient equipment (Jitte, Spider-Suit, auto-attaching Mattock), Mjölnir that doubles as removal and equips cheaply onto its many legendary Dwarves, plus seven burn spells for interaction, all on a mana base that supports the gold two-drops. Deck A has real power with Leyline Axe and Thorin, Mountain-king, but it runs zero removal spells, includes dead slots like Doc Ock's Tentacles with no 5-drops to trigger it and an off-tribe Raubahn, and has clunky 4-mana equip costs and a 23-land count that make its draws far more inconsistent.

Deck A is the tighter build: a low curve of Dwarves, equipment that Kíli and Mauler actually make cheap, Mattock auto-attaching, and seven cheap burn spells so it can interact instead of just racing. Deck B has real upside in free Leyline Axes and Thorin, Mountain-king as removal, but it runs 15 equipment with zero spells, four copies of a 4-mana legend, and Doc Ock's Tentacles that can never auto-attach since nothing in the deck is mana value 5+, so it floods on redundant gear and folds to any disruption.

Deck B is a clean mono-black sacrifice shell: 22 black sources that never miss, recursive fodder (Bloodghast, Forsaken Miner, Nine-Lives Familiar) feeding Zealot/Egotist/Rat King, and seven real removal spells so it can actually interact. Deck A has the higher-ceiling payoffs in Rottenmouth Viper and Obsessive Pursuit, but it is a three-color deck of one- and two-drops with only ~9 red sources for a four-of RG two-drop, heavy self-inflicted life loss from shocks, Starting Town, Pursuit and Inspector, and very little interaction, so it will stumble far more often in a tournament than B.

Deck B has real Standard-caliber payoffs for a sacrifice shell — Rottenmouth Viper closes games off cheap fodder, Lively Dirge rebuys the value creatures, and Biotech Specialist plus Sackville-Bagginses turn every Treasure/Clue/Lander into real reach — alongside Clue-based card advantage from Obsessive Pursuit. Deck A's mana is flawless but the deck is a pile of 1-drops draining for one at a time with almost no card advantage and a weak top end. B's three-color mana with an RG two-drop is its main liability, but Gene Pollinator and the fastland/shockland/Verge base make it workable enough that the power gap decides it.

Deck B is a coherent Boros walkers shell: a clean 24-land all-dual/basic mana base, cheap efficient removal (Burst Lightning, Sear, Helix, Get Lost, Solitary Cell), Voice of Victory to shield planeswalkers from instant-speed interaction, and Solitary Cell turning redundant legendary walkers into cards. Deck A is unfocused—Day of Judgment fights its own token plan, three copies of a legendary enchantment and scattered 1-ofs, and a mana base full of colorless Fountainports, tapped Sunken Citadels and Verges with too few basics/Foundries to reliably cast RR and WW spells.

Deck A is a focused, tight RW planeswalker shell: 24 solid dual-heavy lands, four Memorial as walker ramp, cheap efficient interaction (Burst Lightning, Helix, Sear, Get Lost, Cell) to protect walkers, and Voice of Victory as a cheap body that also stops opposing instant-speed answers on your turn. Deck B is cluttered with speculative one-ofs (Mind Stone, Iceberg, Spark Hunter), anti-synergistic Day of Judgment alongside token-makers and Caretaker's Talent, weak removal like Erode, and a shaky mana base with Fountainports, Sunken Citadels, and Cori Mountains plus only four basics that will struggle with WW/RR costs.

Deck B is the tighter, more cohesive mono-green build: it pairs the dork/Trudge/Badgermole ramp with real card advantage (4 Kiora, 4 Outcaster Trailblazer, 3 Henge) and threats that scale on their own (Ouroboroid, Ghalta, Craterhoof), plus Boseiju for interaction. Deck A drowns in mana sources (12 dorks plus 22 lands) while leaning on 8 clunky tutor effects for a handful of awkward one-ofs like Emrakul and Summon: Bahamut, giving it too few ways to draw cards and a slow, inconsistent top end.

Deck A is the more coherent devotion/ramp shell: eight one-drop dorks into Kiora, Outcaster Trailblazer and Ouroboroid give it real card flow and snowball with Fight Rigging and Henge, Kiora untapping Nykthos/Henge is a proven engine, and the Rhythm/Hoof/Ghalta top end is castable. Deck B leans on clunky bricks (Emrakul that never gets cheap in a mono-green graveyard, a nine-mana Bahamut, Titan) that only work off a Fight Rigging hideaway hit, has no draw engine outside Henge, and runs seven tutors for a thin, awkward target suite. A's only real miss is running two Nykthos instead of four, which is less damaging than B's structural problems.

Deck A is essentially the proven Pioneer Boros Heroic shell: Hoplite/Virtuoso/Swiftspear backed by Monstrous Rage, Ancestral Anger, Reckless Rage and Sheltered by Ghosts gives it haste, trample, removal and card flow with a clean 20-land Boros manabase, even if Speedball and Academic Dispute are odd includes and it is light on cheap protection. Deck B leans on four Homestead Courage, which is a Modern Horizons 2 card and not Pioneer legal, plays four clunky 3-mana Practiced Offense, and mixes non-heroic Hallowblade and colorless Mutavaults into a WW Phalanx Leader deck, making it both less legal and less consistent.

Deck B is essentially the proven Pioneer Boros Heroic shell: Swiftspear, Hoplite, and Virtuoso backed by Monstrous Rage and Ancestral Anger give it haste, trample, and real card flow, and the 20-land Boros mana base (Foundry, Pathway, Vantage, Forge, Confluence) is clean. Speedball and Reckless Rage are questionable slots and 14 creatures is a touch low, but it still closes games far faster than Deck A, which is a pile of sorcery-speed +1/+1 counters with only six protection spells, no evasion or reach, WW costs fighting Mutavault, and Hero of Iroas with just four auras.

Deck B is a coherent four-color control shell: No More Lies, Supreme Verdict, Sear, Get Lost and The Wandering Emperor give it real answers to both creatures and noncreature threats plus an actual win condition beyond Revelation tokens, and 26 lands plus 4 Tablets is the right amount of mana for a seven-drop top end. Deck A runs 27 lands with zero counterspells, weak removal like Erode and Fiery Impulse, a singleton Together as One gimmick, and no proactive threats, so it floods and has no way to interact with Pioneer's noncreature combo and ramp decks. B's mana is fragmented but functional with ample white/blue and enough black for three Inevitable Defeat.

Deck A is a coherent Pioneer control shell: No More Lies gives it answers to noncreature threats and combo, Supreme Verdict is a real 4-mana sweeper, The Wandering Emperor adds a flash threat/removal, and its removal suite (Helix, Sear, Get Lost, Inevitable Defeat) covers more ground. Deck B has zero counterspells, leans on 6-mana Farewell as its only sweeper, plays Erode (ramping the opponent) and a clunky Together as One, and runs 4 Inevitable Defeat on only ~9 black sources with several conditional/tapped lands. A's mana is a bit of a patchwork of one-ofs but still produces all colors adequately, and its plan hangs together far better.

Deck B is essentially the proven Pioneer UR Terror/Crab shell—12 one-mana cantrips, real cheap removal (Fiery Impulse, Burst Lightning, Lightning Axe), Spell Pierce, and 19 lands—so it actually interacts with Pioneer's aggro and combo decks while turning on its threats fast; the green splash for Bushwhack is a questionable concession but the mana (8 green sources for a one-drop sorcery) is workable. Deck A has almost no interaction, only 8 real threats, and leans on clunky engine pieces like four Boomerang Basics and Up the Beanstalk that only triggers off 12 cards, with a thin 18-land base, which a strong player would not trust in a tournament.

Deck A is a coherent Izzet Terror shell: 23 cheap cantrips/removal fuel Terror and Crab fast, Fiery Impulse/Burst Lightning/Lightning Axe actually stop Pioneer aggro, and Spell Pierce/Prismari Charm give real interaction, with Bushwhack doubling as a fight removal spell for a 5/5. Deck B's Beanstalk/Cache Grab plan is cute but it runs zero true removal or counters, four Boomerang Basics and Analyze the Pollen are weak tempo filler, Cache Grab mills creature cards it can't recur, and 18 lands with a pile of sorceries is shaky. A's green splash is a little greedy (8 green sources, only 3 basics to Bushwhack for), but it still does the job far better than B.

Deck A is a coherent Persist reanimator shell: Street Wraith/Troll cycling, Stitcher's Supplier, Overlord milling and Eyetwitch learn all put Archon in the yard, and it has three distinct ways to bring it back (Persist, Emperor of Bones, Overlord recursion) plus Crypt of Agadeem/Phyrexian Tower to hard-cast or ramp, with a tight mono-black mana base. Deck B is a muddled aristocrats/reanimator hybrid where only Persist actually reanimates, Detective's Phoenix's collect evidence fights with the graveyard plan, Bloodghast and four draw-two sac spells don't advance the Archon game plan, and 18 lands plus a two-color base is shakier.

Deck A runs four Faithless Looting, which is banned in Modern, so it isn't even tournament-legal, and it also only has 18 lands with a Detective's Phoenix plan that eats the very graveyard Persist needs. Deck B is a coherent, legal Persist/Emperor of Bones shell: Stitcher's Supplier, Street Wraith and Troll cycling fill the yard, Overlord of the Balemurk and Emperor give redundant ways to get Archon back, and Phyrexian Tower/Crypt of Agadeem make the mana actually support both sacrifice outlets and hardcasting. The numbers and 19-land base plus Boggart Bog MDFCs are sound for a strong player.

Deck B is the coherent, known Modern Eldrazi Ramp shell: Utopia Sprawl/Halfling/Talisman accelerate into Trudge and Fight Rigging, Turntimber Symbiosis doubles as land and a hit, and the top end (3 Emrakul, 2 Sire, Devourer) is sized sensibly with 23 land-equivalents and 9 Forests for Sprawl. Deck A jams 4 legendary Emrakul plus Ulamog and Ugin on thin green mana, and its Green Sun's Zenith package is weak here—Mycospawn is devoid so GSZ can't find it, Trudge off GSZ enters with three stun counters, and Gemstone Caverns/Mosswort Bridge are filler—so the plan doesn't hang together as well.

Deck B is the coherent, proven shape of the archetype: 4 Ugin's Labyrinth with ten colorless 7+ imprint targets (4 Emrakul, 2 Ulamog, 2 Ugin, 2 Drowner), Green Sun's Zenith turning Dryad Arbor/Fanatic of Rhonas/Trudge/Disciple into a consistent ramp-and-refuel engine, and Fanatic plus a 5/5 Trudge producing explosive GGGG turns. Deck A dilutes the plan with low-impact mana sources (Talisman, Halfling, Utopia Sprawl on only 9 Forests), runs just 3 Labyrinths against a mere six imprintable cards, and has a weaker, lower-count top end (3 Emrakul, Sire, Devourer) with no tutor to find it, so its Fight Rigging and Labyrinth payoffs misfire far more often.

Deck A is the coherent, proven Riddlesmith/Echo of Eons shell: Ancient Tomb and Urza's Saga power out Riddlesmith plus a pile of free artifacts, Does Machines and Artist's Talent keep the loot chain going, Gamble/LED set up flashback Echo, Defense Grid and Hexing Squelcher protect the turn, and Grapeshot with Talent level 3 closes. Deck B stitches the Riddlesmith engine onto an ANT skeleton, and the pieces pull against each other: Rituals and Brainstorms don't trigger Riddlesmith, the creature-based loot plan is slow and fragile in a deck that wants to go off in one turn, and the cut to 3 LED/3 Echo weakens the actual combo. Deck A's mana is a bit light on blue, but its plan hangs together far better than B's hybrid.

Deck B is the coherent, proven shape of the Legacy Riddlesmith/Echo of Eons artifact deck: Ancient Tomb and Urza's Saga give it explosive colorless mana and a tutor for its zero-drops, Does Machines and Gamble reliably bin Echo for flashback, Defense Grid and Hexing Squelcher answer the Force of Will/Daze-heavy field, and Artist's Talent plus Grapeshot gives a real kill. Deck A awkwardly splices Riddlesmith onto a Dark Ritual/Infernal Tutor Tendrils shell with no Tomb/Saga acceleration, a thin 13-land base, a lone Tendrils with only three tutors, and competing plans that make it both slower and more fragile than a dedicated ANT or PO list.

Deck A is the proven Legacy Phoenix shell: Dark Ritual/Petal into turn-one Buried Alive, cheap cantrips to trigger Phoenix, and The Fantasticar as a second threat that dodges graveyard hate while rewarding the same noncreature-spell density, backed by real Legacy interaction in Thoughtseize, Daze and Force. Deck B leans on Modern-style filler like Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot and Lava Dart, which are weak in Legacy, has no plan B beyond four Phoenixes, and Lava Dart's Mountain-sacrifice flashback strains a 16-land manabase; the free-spell count alone doesn't compensate for the lack of disruption and resilience.

Deck B is essentially the proven Legacy Grixis Phoenix shell: Buried Alive + Dark Ritual into Flow State/cantrip chains, backed by Thoughtseize and Daze to force the combo through and The Fantasticar as a colorless backup threat that dodges graveyard hate and wins on its own off the same four-spell turns. Deck A is a purer glass cannon padded with low-impact free spells (Mutagenic Growth, Gut Shot, Lava Dart) that only exist to count toward the Phoenix trigger, has no disruption beyond Force, and folds to a single Surgical or Leyline; its 16-land mana works, but the plan is far less resilient.

Deck B is a coherent Boros Synthesizer/metalcraft shell: 15 artifact lands plus Drum, Ornithopter, Synthesizer and Clues turn Ardent Recruit and Galvanic Blast on reliably, Glint Hawk and Skyfisher rebuy Inspectors/Synthesizers, and Bolt/Blast/Journey/Thraben Charm give it real interaction and reach against Pauper's field. Deck A is an all-in go-wide pile with no removal, fragile 0/1 and 0/3 bodies, four copies of a legendary Leonardo, and Ramosian Rally as its only payoff, so it folds to any sweeper or blocker-heavy board. A strong player would take B's proven, well-built list with a functional 18-land mana base over A's glass cannon.

Deck A is a coherent Boros metalcraft shell: 11 artifact lands plus Drums, Thopters, Synthesizers and Clues reliably turn on Ardent Recruit and 4-damage Galvanic Blast, while Glint Hawk/Skyfisher rebuy Synthesizer and Clue value, and 8 burn spells plus Journey give it real interaction with 18 lands supporting a sane curve. Deck B is an all-creatures pile with zero removal, 14 lands (only 4 of them artifacts) and a fragile swarm of 1/1s and 0/x bodies that folds to Electrickery, Breath Weapon or Fiery Cannonade, and the Leonardo/Spider-Man/Interceptor package is clunky rather than a real payoff. A strong player takes the proven, interactive build.

Deck B is a coherent Boros aggro shell where every piece pulls in the same direction: cheap multicolored creatures keep rebuying the Eidolons, while Lava Dart flashback, Lunarch's disturb and Eidolon recursion all feed Spirit Mascot, backed by real interaction in Bolt and Journey on a sensible 18-land base. Deck A tries to splice the Tireless Tribe/Inside Out combo onto Mascot and four-mana Eidolons plus a graveyard-only Sneaky Snacker, leaving it with too many clunky bodies, only one Fling, almost no removal, and a plan that folds to a single answer in a fast format.

Deck B actually builds an engine around cards leaving the graveyard: discard outlets (Tribe, Axe, Looting, Pursue, Discovery) pitch Sneaky Snacker and the Eidolons, Snacker recurs for free off Thrilling Discovery/Looting draws, and every return pumps Spirit Mascot, with Tireless Tribe + Inside Out/Fling as a real backup kill. Deck A is a pile of low-impact Boros bodies (Recruit, Halberdiers) with six clunky 4-mana Eidolons on 18 lands, so its 'aggro' plan and its curve fight each other and it has no late-game edge beyond Bolt.

Deck A is a coherent Premodern Rector Control list: Explorer ramps and fixes a four-color manabase, Innocent Blood/Cabal Therapy/Phyrexian Tower reliably kill Rector into Decree of Silence or Deed, and FoF/Impulse/Blessing/Tusker smooth draws while Swords and Deed handle the board. Deck B stuffs 3 Future Sight (UUU) and Goblin Bombardment into a green Survival creature shell with only 3 Islands and 1 Mountain, has no real removal, and its Survival/Pattern/Rector/Bombardment pieces don't converge on a clean finishing line, so it's a strained mishmash rather than a plan.

Deck B is a coherent, 60-card Rector/Explorer control shell: Innocent Blood, Therapy and Phyrexian Tower all double as Rector sac outlets, Decree of Silence and Deed are real lock pieces, and Swords/Blood/Deed give it actual interaction while Explorer and Tusker make the four-color mana reliable. Deck A is 61 cards in five colors trying to cast triple-blue Future Sight off three Islands and WW Karmic Guide off two Plains, runs zero removal beyond Bombardment, and its Survival toolbox doesn't converge on a convincing kill, so it folds to disruption and its own mana far more often.

Deck A is a coherent Survival/Sneak Attack shell: 8 dorks and 22 lands support the engine, Squee gives a repeatable Survival loop, the discard suite plus Mesmeric Fiend protects the combo and fuels Therapy, and Sneak Attack cheats real haymakers like Dragon Tyrant and Nicol Bolas past their costs. Deck B is a reanimator deck whose only targets are four Bloodfire Colossus and a Symbiotic Wurm, which are poor reanimation payoffs (Colossus hits you too and Reanimate costs 8 life), Survival has almost nothing to find, 4 Rhystic Tutor is unreliable, and 16 lands with Gemstone Mines is a shaky base for a deck that wants to grind with Survival.

Deck B is a real Survival/Sneak Attack shell: 8 dorks and 22 lands make Survival turn two routine, Squee and Genesis give the engine fuel, and Sneak into Dragon Tyrant (12 flying double-strike trample) or Nicol Bolas (hand discard) ends games fast, with 8 discard spells plus the Mesmeric Fiend/Therapy exile trick for protection. Deck A is a reanimator deck whose only real target is Bloodfire Colossus (an 8-life Reanimate for a vanilla 6/6 that needs R to do anything), with only 5 fatties for Buried Alive/Survival, four weak Rhystic Tutors, and a painful 16-land base that compounds the Reanimate life loss.
